In PHP, when the boolean value `false` is cast to a string, it results in an empty string (`""`), whereas `true` becomes `"1"`.

ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character uppercased; it does not modify the original string in place.
Heredoc syntax (<<<EOF) supports variable interpolation and escape sequences, whereas nowdoc syntax (<<<'EOF') treats the content as a literal string without interpreting variables.

PHP automatically converts string keys that represent valid integers, such as '5', into integer keys when storing them in arrays.

In PHP's weak typing mode, a numeric string like "5" is automatically coerced to the integer 5 when passed to a function expecting an int.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing properties to be declared directly in the constructor signature.
The final keyword in PHP prevents a method from being overridden in child classes.
In PHP, the 'final' keyword is used to prevent a method from being overridden by a subclass.
Private properties in a parent class are not accessible in a subclass; only public and protected properties are.

In PHP, attempting to reassign a readonly property throws a readonly property Error.
In PHP, interfaces can define constants that are publicly accessible and immutable.
The instanceof operator in PHP checks if an object is an instance of a specific class or interface.
In PHP, interfaces can declare static methods, which are then implemented as static methods in the implementing class.

The instanceof operator in PHP checks both class inheritance and interface implementation, so an object instance of a class implementing an interface will return true when checked against that interface.
In PHP, interface methods must be abstract and cannot have a body or default implementation, unlike trait methods.
Abstract methods in PHP can indeed be declared with protected, public, or private visibility, although private is rarely used.
The enum Foo has three cases (A, B, and C), so Foo::cases() returns an array containing these three cases.
In PHP, the Throwable interface is implemented by both the Exception and Error classes (and their respective child classes), making it their common ancestor.
In PHP, TypeError extends Error, not Exception, so it is not caught by a catch (Exception $e) block.
In PHP, the @ operator only suppresses errors (E_NOTICE, E_WARNING, E_DEPRECATED, E_USER_NOTICE, E_USER_WARNING), not exceptions.
Since PHP 8.0, the intdiv() function throws a DivisionByZeroError when the divisor is zero, replacing the previous ArithmeticError.
In PHP, the finally block is executed after the try and any caught catch blocks, regardless of whether an exception is caught or propagates further up the call stack.
In PHP, if an exception is thrown within a finally block, it replaces any exception that was previously propagated from the try or catch block, thus affecting the final result.
Shutdown functions registered with register_shutdown_function() are executed when the script terminates, including cases where exit is called.
The 'use' statement is purely an alias for the current scope and does not trigger autoloading or load the class file.
In PHP, the 'use' keyword is followed by 'function' to import a function alias (e.g., 'use function My\Namespace\myFunc as alias;').
PSR-4 converts the remaining namespace parts (Controller\Api\) into directories and appends the class name (UserController) with the .php extension to the base path (src/).
Composer's generated vendor/autoload.php script internally calls spl_autoload_register() to register its autoloader.
The magic constant __NAMESPACE__ contains the name of the current namespace at compile time, and it returns an empty string if in the global namespace.
In PHP, an unqualified class name in a `new` expression is resolved from the current namespace, not the global root.
PSR-4 mapping converts namespace separators to directory separators, so App\Model\User maps to src/Model/User.php.
In PHP, use statements (for classes, functions, or constants) placed inside a function or method scope are local to that scope and do not affect the global namespace or other scopes.
In PHP, arrays are passed by value, meaning a copy is made when assigning them to another variable.
Arrays in PHP are copied by value when assigned, so modifying $b does not affect $a.
In PHP, local variables inside a function do not automatically see global variables unless explicitly accessed via the global keyword, $GLOBALS array, or by being passed as arguments.
The $GLOBALS array represents the global scope; unsetting a key from it removes the variable globally, not just locally.

A foreach loop by value iterates over a snapshot of the array's values at the time of loop initialization, so modifications to the original array inside the loop do not affect the current iteration's sequence.
In PHP, static properties are associated with the class itself rather than specific objects, meaning all instances of the class share the same single copy of that property.
In PHP, boolean keys in arrays are automatically converted to integers (true becomes 1, false becomes 0), so a key cannot be stored as a boolean type.
In PHP generators, returning a value sets the return value that can be retrieved using the Generator::getReturn() method after the generator is exhausted.
In PHP, calling rewind() on a generator allows it to be traversed again, effectively resetting its iteration state.
In PHP, the yield from construct is used to delegate iteration to another generator or iterable, allowing nested generators to yield values as if they were part of the parent generator.
In PHP, calling get_class on a generator object returned by a function using yield returns the string 'Generator'.
The generator yields three integers (1, 2, 3), which are converted to an array with three elements.
SplStack implements a LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) stack, not a FIFO queue; SplQueue is used for FIFO operations.
The ArrayIterator class in PHP implements the Iterator, IteratorAggregate, ArrayAccess, and Countable interfaces, allowing for the traversal and manipulation of arrays.
ArrayObject implements the Traversable interface, so it can be iterated using foreach.
In PHP, the password_hash() function automatically generates a salt and incorporates it into the returned hash string; there is no separate parameter to provide a salt.
PASSWORD_DEFAULT in PHP 8 uses the bcrypt algorithm (cost 10), not md5.
password_verify() returns true when the plain text password matches the hash generated by password_hash().
strip_tags() removes HTML tags, not SQL-specific characters, so it does not protect against SQL injection.
session_regenerate_id() creates a new session ID and invalidates the old one, which prevents attackers from hijacking sessions by using a known ID (session fixation).
session_destroy() removes the session data from the server-side storage, but it does not automatically delete the session ID cookie on the client's browser.
The $_SESSION superglobal is only populated and accessible after calling session_start() (or session_create_id and session_start in newer contexts).
PHP returns 'class@anonymous' as the class name for anonymous classes.
Traits in PHP allow defining constants, which become part of the class that uses the trait.
In PHP, any object (including instances of Exception) is cast to true when converted to a boolean, regardless of its internal state.

PHP 8.4 introduced first-class property hooks, allowing get, set, and unset logic to be defined directly within the property declaration.
Asymmetric visibility for properties was introduced in PHP 8.4.
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.4 to suggest that a function's return value should not be discarded.
The pipe operator (|>) was introduced as a new feature in PHP 8.4.
The clone-with syntax was introduced in PHP 8.4.
The array_first() and array_last() functions were added in PHP 8.4.
